cim: 'Anthropic's IPO is likely driven more by fear than faith in the AI future'
cim_eredeti: 'Anthropic's IPO is likely driven more by fear than faith in the AI future'
szoveg_eredeti:
Ever since the dot-com era of the late 1990s, Silicon Valley startups went public later and larger. Insiders and investors preferred to stay private longer, maintaining founder-mode control and retaining larger shares of a technology's value creation. Uber, Airbnb, and Palantir went public 10, 12, and 17 years after founding. Stripe and Databricks, founded in 2010 and 2013, still shun public markets.

Against this pattern, Anthropic's decision to go public a scant three years into its technology and business development journey – in the face of mounting uncertainties, instability, and deepening backlash – is anomalous and curious. For one thing, the incessant distractions and myopic scrutiny of public markets make them an inhospitable laboratory for the continuous, iterative experimentation that AI products, business, governance, and risk-management models at this early stage demand.

Why, then, is Anthropic going public right now?

Access to growth capital can't be the rationale. Private capital is abundant and remarkably cheap. Venture, private-equity, institutional, and sovereign-wealth funds plough billions into high-growth startups, even at steep valuations once reserved for Wall Street darlings, as they compete for a stake in the AI revolution. Indeed, the emergence of growth-stage venture financing represents a profound shift in the financing of technology innovation. Looking for proof? Consider Anthropic's $65 billion private investment round in May.

Nor could liquidity be the motivation. Founders, funders, and early employees of frothy startups can trade shares in private markets, cashing out long before a company goes public. This IPO is puzzling. The compounding convergence of major risk factors suggests it is likely driven more by fear than faith in the AI future.

First, the business risk. While corporate AI spending eclipses other capex categories, return on investment in AI remains, at best, uncertain. Quantifying its impact on creativity, innovation, productivity, and performance – while accounting for the unintended effects on the workforce, including chronic anxiety, cognitive inertia, worker isolation, and the crowding out of genuine collaboration – will require years-long data and research. Currently, the return on investment on AI is entirely unknowable.
